title: Evolution's Repeat Trick: Same Leaf, Different Genes
summary:
The Galápagos Islands have been a living laboratory for evolution ever since Charles Darwin visited in 1835. Now, a new study reveals an even more surprising twist: plants there evolved the same leaf shape multiple times, but each time using different genes.

Researchers studied Scalesia, a group of plants known as Galápagos giant daisies. These plants are relatively young—all existing species emerged in the past million years. Yet they've adapted to wildly different habitats, from humid highland forests to hot, dry lowlands. Their appearance varies dramatically, from low shrubs to tall trees. Most striking are the leaves, which range from large and smooth to small and deeply lobed, with intricate serrated edges.

Scientists suspected these lobed leaves help plants survive dry conditions by limiting water loss and releasing heat. But the genetic mechanism was unknown.

The team, led by Vanessa Bieker of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, and Professor Michael D. Martin of NTNU, analyzed the complete genomes of every known Scalesia species. Their results, published in Nature Communications, showed that deeply lobed leaves evolved independently several times in separate branches of the family tree. And each time, it was driven by different genes—even though they all belong to the same biological system controlling leaf development.

"This provides a clear example of parallel evolution: nature arriving at the same solution multiple times, but through different genetic pathways," says Bieker. Instead of relying on a single 'master gene,' evolution draws on an entire network of interacting genes, tweaking different components to produce similar outcomes.

The discovery gives scientists a clearer picture of how complex features can repeatedly emerge in unrelated populations or in different branches of the same evolutionary family. It also suggests that new species may currently be developing—numerous Scalesia populations could represent separate evolutionary lineages not yet formally recognized.

This echoes Darwin's finches, which evolved different beak shapes to exploit different food sources. The Galápagos continue to reveal new biology, more than 150 years after Darwin's groundbreaking work. As Martin puts it, "these islands continue to reveal new biology."
why_it_matters: This study challenges the idea that similar traits always trace back to the same genetic cause. For a 12- to 14-year-old learning about genetics and evolution, it shows that life can tinker and rewire its circuitry in surprising ways. Understanding that flexibility could help us predict how crops or wild species might adapt to a rapidly changing climate.

background_read: Charles Darwin’s 1835 visit to the Galápagos helped him develop the theory of evolution by natural selection. The islands are famous for adaptive radiation, where a single ancestor gives rise to many species adapted to different niches. Darwin’s finches, with their varied beaks, are the best-known example. Now Scalesia—a genus of daisies that can grow as trees or shrubs—offers a plant version of that story. The research team from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (a major botanical research institution in the UK) and NTNU (the Norwegian University of Science and Technology) used whole-genome sequencing to compare every known Scalesia species. Their findings, reported in Nature Communications (a high-impact scientific journal), add a twist: the same leaf shape evolved via different genetic routes. This deepens the debate about whether evolution is predictable and how flexible genetic networks can reshuffle to produce similar appearances.

perspectives.description: The discovery celebrates how evolution can repeatedly arrive at a successful design through different molecular means. It underscores the power of genome sequencing to reveal hidden histories and shows that even well-studied places like the Galápagos still hold secrets, reinforcing the value of biodiversity and conservation.

Focusing on genetics might overlook how the physical environment directly shapes leaf form through plasticity, not just inherited genes. Additionally, lab-based genome studies can struggle to replicate the complex interactions in wild ecosystems; not all evolutionary forces are captured in DNA sequences alone. The risk is overattributing leaf shape to genetic determinism.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical (parallel vs. convergent evolution debate)
perspectives.description: The line between parallel and convergent evolution is blurry. Because Scalesia species share a common ancestor and the same developmental toolkit, some argue this is ‘parallelism’ rather than unrelated convergence. The study illustrates that similar traits can emerge from different tweaks in a shared genetic network, adding nuance to how we classify evolutionary repeatability.

If many Scalesia populations are unrecognized species, conservation laws may need updating to protect them. The work also paves the way for ‘evo-devo’ studies (evolutionary developmental biology) that link changes in gene regulation to visible traits. Similar genome-scale approaches on other island radiations could reveal whether parallel genetic evolution is the rule or the exception.
